title: Price stability objective: two-page evaluation summary (May 2026)
summary: A ready-made frame for judging whether policy has delivered price stability, with the March 2026 CPI and May 2026 cash rate in one place.
lede: Defines price stability as low, stable inflation around 2-3%, then sets out the indicators (CPI, monthly CPI, trimmed mean, cash rate), the policies (monetary, fiscal, supply-side) and a judgement step. It concludes headline inflation of 4.6% is above the band while underlying inflation is within it, and the RBA raised the cash rate to 4.35% on 6 May 2026.

terms.def: Low, stable and predictable inflation, not zero inflation.
An underlying inflation measure that strips out the most volatile price changes.
The delay between a policy change and its full effect on the economy.

angle: Use the identify-indicators-analyse-trade-offs-judge steps as the skeleton of any 'evaluate the success of policy in achieving price stability' response, quoting the headline versus underlying gap.

questions.q: Distinguish between headline and underlying inflation.
Explain one trade-off of using higher interest rates to achieve price stability.

title: Full employment objective: two-page evaluation summary (May 2026)

lede: Defines full employment, lists the key indicators (unemployment rate, participation rate, employed persons, job vacancies) and the fiscal, monetary and supply-side policies used, then walks through analysis, trade-offs and a verdict. It quotes an unemployment rate of 4.3%, participation of 66.8% and 214,800 job vacancies, and puts the long-run average unemployment rate at 6.1%.

title: Environmental sustainability objective: checklist and indicators (2026)
summary: A one-page checklist for evaluating policy against the environmental sustainability objective, with the renewables share and the 2035 emissions target.
lede: Defines environmental sustainability as growth that protects the environment and future living standards, lists policy examples (emissions-reduction policy, the Safeguard Mechanism, the energy transition) and indicators, and rates progress 'improving but incomplete'. It notes renewables were 36% of Australia's electricity in 2024 and that emissions fell in the year to June 2025 but more cuts are needed for the 2035 target of 62-70% below 2005.

terms.def: Development that meets current needs without harming future generations' capacity to meet theirs.
Policy that limits emissions from Australia's largest industrial facilities.

angle: Use the define-policy-data-mechanism-lags-judgement sequence, citing the renewables share and target gap to argue policy is partly successful.

questions.q: Explain how a market-based instrument can improve environmental sustainability.

title: Evaluating policy success in Australia: indicators and trends (2026)
summary: A quick reference of what success looks like for each economic objective, with benchmark ranges for inflation, unemployment and growth.
lede: Sets out Australia's key economic objectives, the indicators and sources to use (ABS, RBA, Treasury) and a method of comparing before and after while controlling for global shocks. It gives benchmarks of inflation 2-3%, unemployment around 4-4.5% or lower and trend GDP growth of 2-3%, with a recent example of policy trade-offs in 2022-24.

terms.def: Gaining on one objective at a cost to another, such as lower inflation but higher unemployment.
A side effect of policy that was not the aim.

angle: Use as the evaluation checklist: match the policy to an objective, track indicators before and after, assess trade-offs, conclude successful, partially successful or not yet.

questions.q: Outline two limitations of using a single indicator to judge policy success.

title: When petrol prices rise, do petrol thefts follow? BOCSAR Bulletin 280 summary
outlets: NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research
summary: A research case study showing the causal effect of a 1% petrol price rise (about +3% thefts) is far smaller than the link between thefts and living costs.
lede: A teacher summary of Adams (2026), Crime and Justice Bulletin No. 280, which tests whether higher petrol prices cause more petrol theft using three models. It finds a causal rise of about 3% in thefts after a 1% price rise, but medium-term associations show theft tracks living costs (6.51) and wages (-16.35) far more than petrol prices (0.94).

figures.label: Rise in petrol thefts from a 1% rise in petrol prices
Elasticity of theft to living costs vs petrol prices
Elasticity of theft to nominal wages

terms.def: An outside factor (here world oil prices) used to isolate a cause that the outcome could not have produced.
The % change in one variable after a 1% change in another.
Variables moving together does not prove one causes the other.
Wages adjusted for price changes.

angle: Show that cost-of-living and falling real income, rather than petrol prices alone, explain behavioural change; use it to discuss effects of inflation on households.

questions.q: Distinguish between correlation and causation using petrol prices and petrol theft.
Analyse what the elasticities 0.94 (petrol) and 6.51 (living costs) suggest about the causes of the rise in thefts in 2022-24.

extended: Analyse the economic and social costs of inflation for the Australian economy, and evaluate the effectiveness of the policies available to government in addressing them. In your answer, refer to the stimulus.
note: Teacher research summary of a NSW Government bulletin. The bulletin is dated August 2026 with no day, so 1 Aug is used as the date. The larger elasticities are associations, not causal effects.
